name: Areli
title: Son of Gad and ancestor of the Arelites
summary: Areli was the youngest son of Gad, who in turn was a son of Jacob and the maidservant Zilpah. As part of Jacob's extended household of seventy persons, he went to Egypt when the family settled in Goshen. Areli became the founder of the clan of the Arelites, which formed one of the seven family groups within the tribe of Gad at the census on the plains of Moab (Num 26:17). Although little is known about Areli as an individual, his place in the genealogies shows that he had lasting significance for the organization and identity of the tribe of Gad.

keyEvents.title: Jacob's Household Moves to Egypt
keyEvents.description: Areli is mentioned among Gad's seven sons in the list of Jacob's descendants who went to Egypt, totaling seventy persons.

keyEvents.title: The Genealogy of the Arelites in the Census
keyEvents.description: During the census on the plains of Moab, Areli's descendants, the Arelites, were registered as a distinct clan group within the tribe of Gad.

versions.summary: Areli was the seventh and youngest son of Gad, who was the son of Jacob and Zilpah. He was one of the seventy persons in Jacob's household who went down to Egypt. He became the ancestor of the Arelite clan among the tribe of Gad.
versions.title: Son of Gad
versions.reason: [minor] Verse 17 refers to the sons of Asher, not the sons of Gad. Areli is mentioned only in verse 16. Verse 27 concerns the total number but is not directly relevant to Areli. It is better to distinguish these references more clearly.; [major] 1 Chronicles 5:15–16 does not mention the sons of Gad as listed in Genesis 46:16. Chapter 5 of 1 Chronicles mentions some of Gad's descendants, but Areli is not explicitly named in verses 15–16. This reference is unreliable and should be removed.; [minor] The summary is good but could be clarified by noting that Areli was the ancestor of the Arelites according to Numbers 26:17.; [minor] 'Patriarch' may be misleading for a relatively unknown figure like Areli. 'Ancestor' or 'founder' would be more precise, since 'patriarch' is usually used for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.; [minor] There are no footnotes on the linguistic meaning of the name 'Areli' and other relevant details.; [minor] The names of the siblings should be verified. In Genesis 46:16, some Norwegian translations have slightly different spellings. 'Sifjon' can also be written as 'Sefon' (cf. Num 26:15). What matters is consistency in the database.

versions.summary: Areli was the seventh and youngest son of Gad, who was the son of Jacob and Zilpah. He was one of the seventy persons in Jacob's household who went down to Egypt. Areli became the ancestor of the Arelite clan, a distinct group within the tribe of Gad, as shown in the census during the wilderness wanderings (Num 26:17).
versions.title: Son of Gad and ancestor of the Arelites
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 in wording and structure. It should be rephrased more distinctly to avoid repetition.; [minor] The first two events overlap significantly – both refer to Gen 46:16. Consider merging them or differentiating them more clearly.; [minor] In the linguistic footnote, the form 'אַרְאֵלִי' (ar'eli) is used, which is the gentilic form (Arelite), not the base form of the name. The base form is 'אַרְאֵלִי' (Areli) or more accurately 'אֲרֵלִי'. Furthermore, 'teofert' is an unusual spelling; it should be 'teofort'.; [major] Sibling names should be carefully verified against the Hebrew text. In Gen 46:16, Gad's sons are listed as: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. The order in the list is correct, but the name forms should be consistent with Norwegian Bible tradition.; [minor] The date 'c. 1850 BC' is a reasonable estimate for the patriarchal period, but the uncertainty is great. A somewhat broader dating such as 'c. 1800–1700 BC' or similar could have been more precise in relation to common chronologies for Jacob's grandchildren and the migration to Egypt.

footnotes.text: The name Areli (Hebrew: אֲרֵלִי) is likely composed of 'ari' (אֲרִי, lion) and 'El' (אֵל, God), and can be interpreted as 'God's lion' or 'hero with God'. This is a theophoric name that connects its bearer with divine strength and protection.

The Arelites are mentioned in the census in Num 26:17 as one of seven clan groups within the tribe of Gad. Such clan divisions had practical significance for military organization during the wilderness wanderings and for the later distribution of land in Canaan.

The tribe of Gad received its inheritance east of the Jordan, in the Gilead region (Num 32). Archaeological surveys in Transjordan have uncovered settlement patterns from the Middle and Late Bronze Ages that some scholars link to early Israelite presence in the area.

According to rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabba 94), the number seventy—the count of those who went to Egypt (Gen 46:27)—carries symbolic meaning and represents completeness, parallel to the seventy nations in the table of nations (Gen 10).

Gad was the son of Jacob and Zilpah, who was Leah's maidservant. Gad's sons formed a significant clan structure, and the tribe's location east of the Jordan gave them a strategically important yet vulnerable position as a border people against neighboring tribes in Transjordan.
